problem.title: On-device visual inspection
problem.context: A manufacturer inspects parts with cameras on 40 production lines across three plants. Each line has two to four cameras attached to an ARM edge computer with a small neural accelerator. Plant networks can be unavailable for days. Inspectors add about 5,000 labels a week, and models are retrained weekly and pushed to devices. The team has two ML engineers and half-time operations support, with a tight infrastructure budget.

requirements.text: Check every part as it passes the camera and signal a defective part to the line operator.
Retrain the model every week from the newly labelled images and roll the new model out to every line.
Collect the images the model was unsure about, or got wrong, so that inspectors can label them.
Each image is classified on the line within 200 ms, so the line never slows down.
When a plant's network is down for up to seven days, its lines keep inspecting with the model they have; the images collected in the meantime are uploaded when the network returns.
A new model reaches every connected line within 24 hours of approval. When a new model misbehaves on a line, the line operator can go back to the previous one within 15 minutes, without the ML team.
Cloud and infrastructure spending stays under 2,000 euros a month.
Three people build and run the system, with no support outside working hours.
The edge computers (an ARM processor with a small neural accelerator) cannot be replaced this year.

points.description: 1. Models run inference on deployed edge modules, while a scheduled process periodically retrains them using production examples selected by active learning for uncertainty or errors. Updated models are released progressively to edge deployments, with rollback available if monitoring reveals problems. 2. Trade-off: This combines predictable retraining and targeted labeling with safer incremental deployment, but scheduled retraining may react slowly to sudden drift. Active-learning selection and progressive rollout add labeling, orchestration, and device-management complexity.

1. Edge modules run inference locally, while production monitoring feeds new or reviewed data into an automated retraining pipeline. Domain experts provide controlled labels, and recovery-oriented release automation tests and deploys updated models while permitting rollback or manual intervention. Trade-off: This combines low-latency, locally deployed inference with continuous improvement and operational recovery flexibility. It gives up some simplicity and autonomy: labeling requires expert effort, retraining and edge releases add operational complexity, and manual recovery can slow restoration.

Models run inference in deployed edge modules, keeping operational inference at the device. Monitoring detects performance degradation or feature drift, triggers federated retraining using exchanged updates rather than personal data, and promotes resulting releases through progressively stricter environment validation and approval gates. Trade-off: This reduces data movement and supports adaptive models with controlled rollout. It gives up simplicity and update speed because federated learning, drift-triggered retraining, and approval gates require coordination and may delay deployment.

1. The system runs inference in deployed edge modules, while scheduled retraining periodically refreshes models using actively selected, uncertain or error-prone production examples. Comprehensive lifecycle traceability records data, experiments, artifacts, runs, and deployment health, and progressive automation releases updates incrementally with rollback. 2. Trade-off: This combines local responsiveness, targeted labeling, auditable governance, and safer deployments, but scheduled retraining may leave newly emerging drift unaddressed until the next cycle, while active labeling and end-to-end traceability add operational coordination and edge releases must accommodate device constraints.

The system runs models locally in deployed edge modules, while domain experts produce and review labeled data for development. Retraining is initiated on a recurring schedule, and release automation deploys updated models with rollback or restoration support plus manual intervention during recovery. Trade-off: Edge inference reduces dependence on runtime connectivity, while scheduled retraining provides predictable operations, but it may miss rapidly changing conditions. Human labeling improves review control, and recovery-oriented releases improve recoverability, at the cost of labeling effort and less fully automatic incident handling.

The system runs models in deployed edge modules, while automated lifecycle workflows coordinate data, infrastructure, and operations. Production inputs that are uncertain or error-prone are selected for labeling, and repository commits trigger tested, staged releases; retraining occurs on a defined recurring schedule. Trade-off: This combines local inference with repeatable delivery and targeted data improvement, but scheduled retraining may delay response to rapid drift. Active-learning selection and edge deployment also add operational coordination and device-management complexity.

1. An edge-deployed system performs on-device inference, uses active learning to select uncertain or error-prone production inputs for labeling, and applies federated learning without centralizing personal training data. Scheduled retraining consumes those labels, while comprehensive lifecycle traceability governs data, runs, artifacts, health, and progressive release automation rolls updates out incrementally with rollback. Trade-off: This gains privacy-preserving learning, targeted labeling, auditable governance, and safer releases, but scheduled retraining may respond slowly to drift, while federated coordination, edge deployment, and integrated traceability increase operational complexity.

1. Models run on deployed edge modules, update incrementally as new data arrives, and undergo additional retraining on recurring schedules. Uncertain or error-prone production inputs are labeled, while integrated lifecycle traceability governs datasets, runs, artifacts, health, and progressively released updates with rollback. 2. Trade-off: This provides local inference, continual adaptation, targeted labeling, auditability, and safer releases, but increases operational and version-management complexity. Scheduled retraining may leave models temporarily stale, while online updates can introduce instability or drift, despite rollback protection.

The system packages models for inference on deployed edge hardware, while human experts produce controlled labels for ongoing development. Scheduled retraining refreshes models, and comprehensive lifecycle traceability records datasets, experiments, runs, artifacts, pipelines, and deployment health; release automation deploys updates and restores prior versions, with manual intervention available during recovery. Trade-off: This improves edge responsiveness, governance, reproducibility, and recoverability, but scheduled triggers may miss rapid drift and edge devices may receive stale models between retraining cycles. Human review and comprehensive tracking also increase operational effort and release complexity.

Deploy models to edge devices, while automated lifecycle workflows use active learning to select uncertain production inputs for labeling and scheduled retraining. Repository commits trigger staged builds, tests, promotion, and deployment, with comprehensive versioning and traceability across pipelines, artifacts, runs, datasets, and deployment health. Trade-off: This combines responsive data-driven improvement and reproducible releases with low-latency, on-device inference. Scheduled retraining may delay adaptation to rapid shifts, while edge deployment and comprehensive traceability increase operational and governance complexity.

The system runs inference on deployed edge devices, while federated learning aggregates model updates without centralizing personal training data. Active learning selects uncertain or error-prone production inputs for labeling, scheduled retraining incorporates them, and traceability governs experiments, artifacts, datasets, health, and progressive releases with rollback. Trade-off: This improves privacy, operational control, auditability, and release safety, but federated coordination and comprehensive governance add complexity. Scheduled retraining may delay responses to newly detected errors, while edge deployment can constrain available runtime resources.

approaches.idea: What if each line keeps inference local, while weekly retraining uses uncertain or incorrect images and releases support rapid rollback?
What if experts control labeling and a recovery-oriented release process handles model incidents?
What if model updates are federated across lines and retraining follows observed drift?
What if lifecycle automation and staged release gates reduce recurring operations across many edge lines?

trajectory.hypothesis: Local inference should keep inspection running during outages and support the latency target; scheduled retraining, active selection, and rollback should fit weekly labels and rollout needs.

tradeoffs.note: Scheduled targeted labeling and progressive rollback support retraining and safer releases, but add coordination for a small operating team.

trajectory.observation: The checked point has no source attesting the combination. Its values align with local inference, recurring retraining, targeted image selection, and rollback, but do not specify a durable offline image queue or the numerical latency and rollback timings.

trajectory.hypothesis: Automation of retraining and expert labeling should preserve review control, while recovery-oriented releases should make restoration possible.

tradeoffs.note: Expert review and manual recovery provide control, but consume staff time and do not select uncertain images or guarantee operator-only rollback.

trajectory.observation: The point is unattested as a combination. The retraining pipeline is automatic but does not specify a weekly trigger, and the labeling value covers label production rather than selecting uncertain or incorrect images.

trajectory.hypothesis: Federated updates and drift detection may keep updates useful across disconnected lines while staged approval controls rollout.

tradeoffs.note: Drift-triggered federated updates avoid centralizing data, but do not ensure weekly retraining from newly labelled images and add coordination for a small team.

trajectory.observation: The combination is unattested. Drift-based triggering does not guarantee the required weekly cadence, while federated updates add coordination without a stated privacy driver. This approach was set aside after the requirement conflict became clear.

trajectory.hypothesis: Add lifecycle traceability to improve reproducibility of weekly training and help identify the deployed model when a line needs rollback.

tradeoffs.note: Integrated tracking helps connect training data, artifacts, and deployment health, but adds governance work for a small team.

trajectory.observation: The checked combination remains unattested. Traceability improves the audit trail, but it does not itself train weekly, buffer disconnected images, or supply the timing guarantees.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replace the general automated retraining trigger with a recurring schedule so the weekly training cadence is explicit.

tradeoffs.note: Recovery automation supports restoration, while manual intervention consumes scarce staff time.

trajectory.observation: The weekly schedule is a closer fit for retraining cadence, but this point still relies on expert labeling and recovery-oriented release intervention. The checked combination is unattested.

trajectory.hypothesis: Add lifecycle automation and staged release gates to reduce repeated work across 40 lines while retaining edge inference and weekly labeling.

tradeoffs.note: Lifecycle automation and staged promotion reduce manual repetition, but this release value does not explicitly provide the previous-version rollback needed for a 15-minute operator recovery.

trajectory.observation: No source attests this combination. It offers broader recurring automation, but staged release gates alone do not state a rollback path or guarantee delivery to every connected line within 24 hours.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replace drift triggering with a weekly schedule and use progressive rollback to address the cadence and recovery concerns found in the federated seed.

tradeoffs.note: Federated updates may use newly labelled examples across lines without centralizing training data, but add coordination without a privacy requirement.

trajectory.observation: The changed schedule and rollback values improve fit for weekly retraining and recovery, but the federated update mechanism remains an extra coordination burden and does not establish the required central labeled-image training workflow. The federated element is not retained in the final alternative.

trajectory.hypothesis: Add incremental updates between weekly retraining cycles to reduce the period a line may use a model that has not incorporated new labels.

tradeoffs.note: Incremental learning may use newly arriving examples sooner, but adds operating complexity and its fit on the fixed ARM accelerator is not established.

trajectory.observation: The point description identifies instability risk from online updates. The space does not establish that incremental training is feasible on the current edge hardware, so this refinement is not preferred over the scheduled-only member.

trajectory.hypothesis: Add lifecycle traceability to make expert-provided labels and recovery actions reproducible.

tradeoffs.note: Traceability improves diagnosis and reproducibility but adds governance work without removing manual label review or recovery handling.

trajectory.observation: Lifecycle traceability strengthens auditability, but the point still does not select uncertain images for inspectors and manual recovery may not meet the operator-only rollback target. It is dominated by the active-selection and progressive-rollback alternative on the stated requirements.

trajectory.hypothesis: Add traceability to the scheduled federated update flow to make its labeled data, model updates, and deployments reproducible.

tradeoffs.note: Federated updates and lifecycle traceability support controlled updates, but add coordination and governance effort.

trajectory.observation: Traceability improves reproducibility, but the point remains more complex than the scheduled central-label path and has no privacy requirement to offset the added coordination. It is dominated by simpler alternatives on the stated requirements.

trajectory.hypothesis: Add lifecycle traceability to the staged automated pipeline so each weekly model and rollout is reproducible across lines.

tradeoffs.note: Automated workflows and traceability reduce repeated manual pipeline work, but staged release automation does not explicitly promise quick restoration of a previous model.

trajectory.observation: The refinement adds traceability but leaves the release tradeoff intact: the point is more automated and auditable, while its rollback fit remains weaker than the progressive-release option. Nothing attests the complete combination.

alternatives.name: Local weekly release with rollback
alternatives.summary: Keep inspection local, use active selection for uncertain or incorrect images, retrain on a recurring schedule, and release progressively with rollback. Trace the training and deployment lifecycle for diagnosis.

choices.reason: Local inference supports line-speed inspection without a live plant network and uses the installed edge computers; this placement appears in Composing Deep-Learning Microservices for the Hybrid Internet of Things and Three Levels of ML Software.
choices.fit_note: The value covers inference placement, but the space does not establish 200 ms performance on this ARM accelerator or specify durable buffering and later upload of collected images.

choices.reason: A recurring trigger matches the required weekly retraining cadence, as described in MLOps: Continuous Delivery and Automation Pipelines in Machine Learning and MLOps Principles.
choices.fit_note: This value specifies when retraining starts, not the training pipeline or rollout to every line.

choices.reason: Active selection targets uncertain or error-prone production inputs for inspector labeling, as discussed in Architecture of a Real-World Machine Learning System and Architecting a Machine Learning System for Risk.

Progressive deployment and previous-version rollback best match a cautious rollout with operator recovery; this is described in Productionizing Machine Learning with a Microservices Architecture and MLOps: Model Management, Deployment, and Monitoring with Azure Machine Learning.
choices.fit_note: The value supports rollback but does not guarantee delivery within 24 hours or operator rollback within 15 minutes.

choices.reason: Lifecycle traceability connects datasets, training runs, artifacts, and deployment health for reproducible releases and diagnosis, as presented in Continuous Intelligence: Moving Machine Learning Application into Production Reliably and MLOps Principles.
choices.fit_note: Traceability supports governance but does not automate training, rollback, or timing guarantees.

considered.reason: Incremental online training was evaluated, but adds instability and hardware feasibility concerns without replacing the required weekly retraining.

open.reason: The space has no choice that specifies durable local image buffering and deferred upload across a seven-day outage.

alternatives.name: Automated staged edge lifecycle
alternatives.summary: Use edge inference and active image selection with scheduled retraining, lifecycle automation, traceability, and commit-triggered staged releases. This reduces repeated operations but leaves quick rollback less explicit.

choices.reason: Local inference supports continued line inspection through network outages, as discussed in Composing Deep-Learning Microservices for the Hybrid Internet of Things and Three Levels of ML Software.
choices.fit_note: The space does not establish the latency on the fixed ARM accelerator or offline image buffering and later upload.

choices.reason: A schedule supports the weekly retraining cadence, as described in MLOps: Continuous Delivery and Automation Pipelines in Machine Learning.
choices.fit_note: The trigger alone does not implement training or prove delivery to every line.

choices.reason: Active learning selects uncertain or error-prone inputs for labeling, as described in Architecture of a Real-World Machine Learning System.

Commit-triggered staged builds and promotion provide repeatable release automation across delivery stages, as described in MLOps: Continuous Delivery and Automation Pipelines in Machine Learning and Continuous Intelligence: Moving Machine Learning Application into Production Reliably.
choices.fit_note: The value supports staged rollout but does not describe rollback or guarantee the required delivery timing.

choices.reason: Automating recurring lifecycle work may reduce repeated manual operations across 40 lines, as discussed in MLOps Principles and MLOps: Model Management, Deployment, and Monitoring with Azure Machine Learning.
choices.fit_note: The value describes lifecycle automation broadly but does not establish staffing needs or operating cost.

choices.reason: Traceability helps connect each model release to its data, run, artifact, and deployment health, as presented in Continuous Intelligence: Moving Machine Learning Application into Production Reliably.
choices.fit_note: It supports reproducibility and diagnosis but does not itself release or restore models.

considered.reason: Progressive release automation with rollback was considered, but this approach favors commit-triggered staged promotion and broader lifecycle automation.

open.reason: The space does not specify a durable offline image queue or deferred upload policy.

adrs.title: Where inspection inference runs
adrs.context: Every part must be classified at line speed, inspection must continue during long plant network outages, and the current ARM edge computers must remain in place. The space supports on-device inference, but provides no measured latency on this hardware and no design for buffering collected images until connectivity returns.

options.name: On-device edge inference
pros: Keeps inference close to the camera and independent of a live plant connection.
cons: The space does not prove 200 ms latency on the fixed ARM accelerator or cover offline image buffering.
options.reason: Both alternatives use the existing edge modules to preserve inspection during outages.

adrs.title: Retraining cadence and label selection
adrs.context: New labels arrive weekly, and inspectors need uncertain or incorrect images. A scheduled trigger best matches the stated cadence, while active learning specifically selects uncertain or error-prone production examples. Neither value alone supplies the full training and rollout pipeline.

options.name: Scheduled retraining with active selection
pros: Matches the weekly cadence and targets production cases for inspector labeling.
cons: Does not itself implement training or state how images are buffered during outages.
options.reason: This pairing directly reflects the stated weekly cycle and uncertainty-driven collection.

options.name: Automated retraining with expert labeling
pros: Automates retraining and gives domain experts controlled label review.
cons: Does not specify a weekly trigger or selection of uncertain and incorrect images.
options.reason: It leaves two explicit functional requirements only partly covered.

options.name: Drift-triggered federated updates
pros: Can react to detected drift and exchanges updates rather than centralizing personal training data.
cons: Does not ensure weekly retraining from newly labelled images and increases coordination.
options.reason: The brief requires a weekly label-driven cycle and gives no privacy constraint that warrants this added approach.

adrs.title: Model rollout and operational control
adrs.context: Approved models must reach connected lines quickly, and operators must restore a previous model without ML-team help. The small operations team favors automation, while rollback and delivery-time targets are more specific than the design-space values.

options.name: Progressive release with rollback
pros: Incremental introduction and prior-version rollback fit the recovery requirement; lifecycle traceability supports diagnosis.
cons: No value guarantees the 24-hour rollout or 15-minute operator rollback targets.
options.reason: This is the closest available fit for rapid and reversible deployment.

options.name: Staged automated lifecycle
pros: Automates recurring workflow and staged build, test, and promotion activities.
cons: Does not explicitly provide rollback and does not guarantee rollout timing.
options.reason: This alternative prioritizes repeatable lifecycle operations across many lines while accepting weaker rollback coverage.

options.name: Recovery release with manual intervention
pros: Supports restoration of a prior version and permits manual recovery actions.
cons: Manual intervention may rely on scarce staff and does not establish operator-only recovery in 15 minutes.
options.reason: It is less aligned with the operator-autonomy and small-team constraints.

unaddressed.note: The space has runtime resource and cost outcomes but no decision value or evidence that estimates or caps cloud and infrastructure spending at 2,000 euros per month.
